Lecture 15-1

When do we choose a fixed bed, and what is inside it?

When a fixed bedParts of the vesselCatalyst and voidsFirst sizing

Lecture 15-1

A fixed bed is a vessel full of catalyst that stays put for months

  1. When a fixed bed is the right reactorcatalyst life, phases, residence time; the industrial scale
  2. The parts of the vesseldistributor, inert layers, catalyst bed, support, outlet collector
  3. The catalyst and the voidspellet shapes, bed void fraction, the wall effect
  4. Diluting and sizing the bedinerts in the catalyst; diameter and length rules

When a fixed bed · step 1 of 2

Choose a fixed bed when the solid catalyst lives for months

Long catalyst life

Life > 3 months. Loading, unloading and start-up take weeks to a month, so the bed must run long between changes.

Any fluid phase

Gas–solid (G/S), liquid–solid (L/S) or gas–liquid–solid (G/L/S) over the same packed solid.

Short residence time

High space velocity: seconds of contact for a gas, so a high throughput per unit of catalyst.

A catalyst that dies in hours needs continuous regeneration: a fluidized bed, as in catalytic cracking.

When a fixed bed · step 2 of 2

Most large catalytic processes run in fixed beds

Basic chemical industryPetrochemical industryPetroleum refining
Steam reforming (primary, secondary)Ethylene oxideCatalytic reforming
Water–gas shift, CO methanationEthylene dichloride, vinyl acetateIsomerization, polymerization
Ammonia synthesisButadiene, maleic anhydride(Hydro)desulfurization
Sulfuric acid (SO2 oxidation)Phthalic anhydride, cyclohexaneHydrocracking
Methanol synthesisStyrene, oxo synthesisHydrodealkylation

After Froment, Bischoff & De Wilde, Chemical Reactor Analysis and Design, 3rd ed. Single-fluid-phase processes only; trickle beds are treated elsewhere.

Single trains now reach about 1.7 Mt/y for methanol and 1.2 Mt/y for ammonia.

Inside every one of these vessels, the same five parts.

Parts of the vessel · click a part

Feed is spread, flows down through inert and catalyst layers, then leaves

Click a part of the vessel

Each part has one job. Together they make the flow through the catalyst as uniform as possible.

Only the catalyst layer reacts; every other part exists to make the flow through it uniform and to keep the catalyst in place.

Before the details: how big and how hot do real fixed beds run?

Industrial scale · from Lecture 10 · filter by thermal configuration

Thirty-seven fixed bed processes: 1–300 bar, 50–1050 °C, up to 205 MW

Configurations 1–6 are the thermal configurations of Lecture 10 (15-2 returns to them). Duty grows with capacity; the multitubular (4) holds the largest heat loads per unit.

Parts · feed distributor

A distributor spreads a single-phase feed over the whole bed top

Slotted: slot area three times the inlet pipe, $a>4$ in. Dish and cone: baffles break the jet.

Parts · inert layers

Graded inert balls hold the catalyst above and below

  • Top layer: stops the catalyst moving, traps scale, helps distribute the feed.
  • Bottom layers: each ball size bridges the one above, so catalyst cannot migrate into the support or collector.
  • For 1/4 in catalyst the first bottom layer is 3 in of 3/8 in balls.

Catalyst · pellet shapes

Spheres, cylinders, rings and lobes: the shape trades area against pressure drop

  • Sphere, cylinder, trilobe (left to right).
  • Small or lobed pellets: short diffusion path, more outer area.
  • Larger, open shapes: higher void fraction, lower pressure drop.

Catalyst · wall effect · try it

In a narrow tube the wall loosens the packing

$$\varepsilon=0.38+0.073\left[1-\frac{(d_t/d_p-2)^2}{(d_t/d_p)^2}\right]$$
$d_t$, $d_p$
tube diameter; particle diameter
m
$\varepsilon$–
above 0.38–

Haughey and Beveridge (1969), spheres, $d_t/d_p>2$. The book prints “+” in the bracket; only “−” returns 0.38 for a wide bed.

Below $d_t/d_p\approx10$ the wall adds voids, so gas bypasses along the wall; above 25 the bed is uniform.

Diluting the bed

Inert particles spread the heat release where the rate is highest

  • Example: the first 5 ft are 20 % catalyst, 80 % inert, both 1/8 in; then at least 2 ft of 1/16 in catalyst.
  • At the inlet the reactant is richest, so the rate and the heat release peak there. Dilution lowers the heat released per bed volume.
  • Same particle size for catalyst and inert: no segregation, uniform flow.

Diluting the catalyst is also the standard cure for a hot spot in a cooled tube.

First sizing · try it

From the catalyst volume to a vessel you can order

$D$ ordered (m)–
bed $L_b$ (m)–
vessel $L$ (m)–
$L_b/D$–
  • Diameter: round up to the next 6 in (0.1524 m).
  • Bed length: $L_b=4V_{cat}/\pi D^2$; keep $L_b\ge D/2$ for an even flow.
  • Vessel length: $L_b$ plus about 3 ft (0.914 m) in total for inert balls at top and bottom, rounded to the next 3 in.

The source slide writes 3 ft as 0.942 m; 3 ft is 0.914 m.

The catalyst volume fixes the product $D^2L_b$; the diameter is the free choice, bounded by flow distribution and, later, by pressure drop.

Parts · outlet

The collector draws product evenly across the bottom

  • A slotted or perforated cylinder sits in 3/4 in balls.
  • Slots spaced around the circumference: equal suction everywhere, no short path through the middle.
  • A catalyst dump nozzle empties the bed at change-out.

Section 15-1 · summary

A fixed bed: long-lived catalyst, held still, flow made uniform

  • Choose it when the catalyst lives > 3 months and contact times are short.
  • Distributor, graded inert layers and collector exist so the flow through the catalyst is uniform.
  • $\varepsilon\approx0.4$; keep $d_t/d_p$ large or the wall adds voids and bypass.
  • $V_{cat}$ fixes $D^2L_b$: pick $D$ (6 in steps), keep $L_b\ge D/2$, add about 3 ft of inerts.

The vessel is fixed. Next: the heat of reaction decides how the beds are arranged.

Lecture 15-2

Which configuration copes with the heat of reaction?

Flow directionAdiabatic temperature riseSix thermal configurations

Lecture 15-2

Flow direction is set by the fluid; heat management by one of six configurations

  1. Three flow directionsdownflow, upflow, radial flow, and what each avoids
  2. Six thermal configurations (Lecture 10)1 adiabatic, 2 exchangers, 3 cold shot, 4 multitubular, 5 added mass, 6 parallel
  3. Staged beds on the x–T mapexchangers against cold shot, under the equilibrium curve
  4. Choosing the configurationby the size and sign of the heat effect, and the total duty

Flow direction

Downflow for gases, upflow for liquids, radial flow for low pressure drop

Vertical downflowVertical upflowRadial flow
Gravity holds the bed: no fluidization. G/S and G/L/S.Keeps the catalyst soaked in liquid. Usually L/S.Short flow path, large flow area: low $\Delta P$, no fluidization.

Flow direction · radial flow

Radial flow keeps the bed thin when the vessel cannot grow wider

  • Gas enters the outer scallops, crosses the annular bed inward, leaves by the centerpipe.
  • Used in catalytic reforming and giant ammonia converters.
  • Why: a recycle compressor sets the allowed $\Delta P$; radial flow raises flow area without a deeper bed.

Heat management follows the six thermal configurations of Lecture 10.

Heat management · Lecture 10 recall

Six ways to handle the heat of reaction

1Single adiabatic reactor

Fixed bed: One adiabatic bed

HT/LT shift, isomerization, methyl chloride

2Adiabatic beds in series + external heating/cooling

Fixed bed: Beds with interstage exchangers or fired heaters

SO3, reforming, NH3 (S-200), methanol

3Adiabatic beds in series + cold/hot shot

Fixed bed: Beds with quench nozzles between them

NH3 and methanol quench converters, solid phosphoric acid (SPA) cumene

4Single isothermal reactor + heating/cooling system

Fixed bed: Multitubular or basket: catalyst in cooled tubes

Phthalic and maleic anhydride, ethylene oxide (EO), Formox, steam reforming

5Single adiabatic + external mass (excess reactant, inert)

Fixed bed: Adiabatic bed with steam or recycle as heat carrier

Styrene (steam), vapour-phase ethylbenzene (EB), methanol-to-gasoline (MTG), substitute natural gas (SNG)

6Isothermal reactors in parallel

Fixed bed: Several multitubular shells side by side

Very large EO or Fischer–Tropsch (FT) duties

Balance $\dot Q_R=\dot Q_1+\dot Q_2$: through the wall ($\dot Q_1$) or carried by the stream ($\dot Q_2$).

Configuration 1 of 6 · single adiabatic reactor

The cheapest fixed bed: a vessel full of catalyst, no wall duty

  • No heat-transfer surface, utility or control loop: every kJ leaves as $\Delta T$.
  • Rule of thumb, exothermic: $\Delta T_{ad}\le0.1\,T_{in}$, both in K.
  • When it fails — endothermic: the bed cools until the reaction dies (reforming, styrene). Exothermic: the rise hurts equilibrium (NH3, CH3OH, SO3), selectivity (maleic anhydride, EO) or catalyst life.

Industrial: HT and LT shift (350–450 and 190–250 °C), isomerization, methyl chloride, the 10–30 mm silver bed for formaldehyde.

Configuration 2 of 6 · adiabatic beds + external heating/cooling

Split the bed; reset the temperature in exchangers between the beds

  • Every bed stays adiabatic; the duty leaves (or enters) in the exchangers between beds.
  • $N$ beds cut the rise about $N$-fold, for $N-1$ exchangers and more $\Delta P$. No more than five beds.
  • Reversible reaction: take each bed to about 90 % of its equilibrium conversion.
  • Endothermic: fired reheaters between beds — naphtha reforming, 3–4 radial beds.

Industrial: SO3 4-bed converter, ammonia S-200, methanol with interchangers, Claus converters.

Configurations 2 and 3 · the conversion–temperature map · try it

Each bed climbs an adiabatic line toward equilibrium, then is cooled

final $x$–
hottest outlet (K)–
cold shot used–

$\Delta T_{ad}$: rise of an adiabatic bed at full conversion. Illustrative $A\rightleftharpoons B$, $\Delta H=-98$ kJ/mol, $K=1$ at 870 K, $E=90$ kJ/mol; cold shot at 450 K.

$\Gamma_e$ caps every bed; the path zig-zags around $\Gamma_m$, the maximum-rate curve. A cold shot cools by dilution, so it also lowers $x$: more beds for the same final conversion.

Configuration 3 of 6 · adiabatic beds + cold/hot shot

One shell, nozzles instead of exchangers: cool by injecting cold feed

  • What resets the temperature is mass, not a wall: cold feed at every gap.
  • Each gap needs a quench distributor and a mixing tray, or hot streaks reach the next bed.
  • Cheaper than configuration 2, but the feed is diluted: each bed converts less, and a failed valve loses the cooling at once.

Industrial: ammonia quench converter (4 beds, 150–300 bar), methanol quench, SO3 shallow beds with cold air, SPA cumene with propylene quench.

Configuration 4 of 6 · single isothermal reactor + heating/cooling system

Remove or add the heat continuously, through thousands of tube walls

  • o-xylene oxidation: up to 20 000 tubes of 2.5 cm i.d., molten salt outside; the small diameter limits the axis overtemperature.
  • Steam reforming (endothermic): tubes 10 cm i.d., 10 m long, heated from 500 to 850 °C at 75.6 kJ/m²s.
  • Also EO, maleic anhydride, Formox, vinyl acetate, Lurgi methanol.

Configuration 4 of 6 · which side holds the catalyst

Catalyst-in-tube for high heat; basket type for moderate heat

Tube in the high-heat case: every pellet sits within half a tube diameter of a cooled wall.

Configuration 4 · construction

Each tube is a small fixed bed with its own support

  • A screen, spring or grid holds the catalyst in every tube.
  • All tubes must be packed alike: equal $\Delta P$, equal flow, equal temperature.
  • Uneven packing is the usual cause of a hot tube.

Configuration 5 of 6 · single adiabatic + external mass

Add mass to the stream so the same heat gives a smaller $\Delta T$

Adiabatic with an added stream$\dot Q_2=\sum_i F_iC_{p,i}(T_{in}-T_{out})+F_mC_{p,m}(T_{m,in}-T_{out})$
  • Styrene: steam/EB 6–12 mol/mol carries the heat and lowers $p_{EB}$. Also vapour-phase EB (benzene excess), MTG, SNG (recycle).
  • Every added kilogram must be separated again: cheap vessel, costly recycle.

Configuration 6 of 6 · isothermal reactors in parallel

Past the wall limit of one shell, repeat the shell

$$N=\left\lceil\frac{\dot Q_R}{\dot Q_{max}}\right\rceil,\qquad A_{unit}=\frac{A_{total}}{N}$$
  • Split the feed evenly: one design, one spare set, clean turndown.
  • $N$ vessels, $N$ control loops: the most expensive option, chosen only when the total duty forces it.

$\dot Q_{max}$: the duty one shell can remove.

Section 15-2 · summary

Flow direction from the fluid, heat management from six configurations

  • Downflow for gases, upflow for liquids, radial flow when $\Delta P$ must stay low.
  • 1 single adiabatic bed when the rise stays within about 10 % of $T_{in}$.
  • 2 exchangers or 3 cold shot between adiabatic beds: the path zig-zags under equilibrium; a cold shot also dilutes.
  • 4 multitubular for strong heat effects; 5 steam or recycle as heat carrier; 6 shells in parallel when one shell is not enough.

Configuration chosen. Next: which model does that bed need?

15-3

Lecture 15-3

Which model does a fixed bed need?

Before writing a single equation: decide which transport steps are fast enough to ignore.

Levels by flow: 1D or 2DLevels by pellet: one phase or twoModel codes A-I to B-IIIRules of thumb

Lecture 15-3

Two questions pick the model: how does the gas mix, and does the pellet differ from the gas?

  1. What a model must predict$C$, $T$, $p$ along the bed, at four scales
  2. Levels by flowplug flow → axial mixing → radial (2D): the I, II, III
  3. Levels by pelletone phase → film → film and pores: the A or B
  4. The model codesA-I … B-III, and which one is used most
  5. Rules of thumb and the tests behind them$L/d_p>50$, $d_t/d_p>25$, $G>1.35$, same pellet as the lab

Scales · step 1 of 2

Three kinds of transport sit between the feed and the active site

Interparticle (bed)Interphase (film)Intraparticle (pellet)
Axial and radial mass and heat dispersionExternal mass and heat transfer, fluid to pellet surfaceInternal diffusion and conduction inside the pores

Scales · step 2 of 2

A model must predict $C$, $p$ and $T$ along $z$, sometimes along $r$

  • Reactant $C_i$ falls along $z$.
  • Pressure $p$ falls by friction.
  • For an exothermic reaction with wall cooling, $T$ rises to a hot spot, then falls.
  • Radius $r$ matters when heat leaves through the wall.

First question: how does the gas move through the packing?

Levels by flow · step 1 of 3

Level 1, plug flow: every slice moves as one, with flat profiles

  • No mixing along or across the tube: only convection, reaction and heat to the wall.
  • One coordinate, $z$: a 1D model. This is the ideal PFR of the earlier lectures.

Levels by flow · step 2 of 3

Level 2: the packing also mixes gas along the bed

$$Pe=\frac{u_i\,d_p}{D_a}=\frac{\text{carried by flow}}{\text{mixed back}}$$
  • Gas swerves round each pellet; some moves back: axial dispersion $D_a$.
  • Gas, $Re>10$: $Pe\approx2$. Liquids: $Pe\approx0.5$; slow lab beds: $Pe\ll1$.
  • Large $Pe$ = plug flow. Same idea as $D/uL$ in Lecture 12, but per pellet.
$u_i$, $d_p$
interstitial velocity $u/\varepsilon$; pellet diameter
m/s, m
$D_a$
axial dispersion coefficient
m²/s

Levels by flow · step 3 of 3

Level 3: a cooled tube is hotter on its axis, so $C$ and $T$ vary with $r$

  • Heat leaves only at the wall; radial mixing $D_r$, $\lambda_r$ carries it out. Two coordinates, $z$ and $r$: a 2D model.
  • Levels 4–5 of the source let velocity vary with $r$ too: research use only.

Second question: is the catalyst at the same $C$ and $T$ as the gas around it?

Levels by pellet · step 1 of 3

Level 1, pseudo-homogeneous: gas and catalyst treated as one phase

  • Film and pores are fast next to the reaction: the rate is evaluated at the bulk $C$ and $T$.
  • One mole balance and one energy balance: models A.

Levels by pellet · step 2 of 3

Level 2: a fast reaction outruns the film, so the surface differs from the gas

  • Gas and catalyst now need separate balances, joined by $k_p$ and $h_p$: model B-I.
  • The surface is usually a few °C hotter than the gas; tens of °C only for very fast exothermic reactions.

Levels by pellet · step 3 of 3

Level 3: large pellets also starve their centre

  • Pore diffusion lowers the rate inside: the pellet balance gives the effectiveness factor $\eta$: model B-II.
  • Only the pores matter? Keep model A and multiply the rate by $\eta$. Inside a pellet $\Delta T$ is rarely over 1–2 °C.

Combine the two answers: flow level gives I, II, III; pellet level gives A or B.

Models · the codes used from here on

Six models: the letter is the pellet level, the numeral the flow level

A · pseudo-homogeneous
one phase, $T_s=T$, $C_s=C$		B · heterogeneous
gas and catalyst apart
1DA-I plug flow — the workhorseB-I plug flow + film
1DA-II + axial mixing $D_a$, $\lambda_a$B-II + film + pores ($\eta$)
2DA-III + radial mixing $D_r$, $\lambda_r$B-III + film, 2D

Careful: II means axial mixing in column A but the pellet interior in column B (Froment’s labels). Each cell adds one effect to the cell above.

Design the bed so the simplest code, A-I, is enough. Four rules do it.

Rules of thumb · gas–solid bed

Four rules keep a fixed bed at model A-I

RuleRemovesReason
$L/d_p>50$, $L/d_t>10$A-II axial mixingmixing reaches a few pellets; a bed of many pellets averages it out
$d_t/d_p>25$; adiabatic, or $d_t\le25$ mm with high $G$A-III radial profileflat velocity; wall heat crosses a thin tube with little $\Delta T$
$G>1.35$ kg/m²s (liquid: 2.7)B-I filmfast gas thins the film around each pellet
same pellet as the kinetic studyB-II poresthe measured rate already contains $\eta$

Each rule is a typical case of a general 5 % test. The next slides show where each number comes from.

Rule 1 · axial mixing · step 1 of 2

$L/d_p>50$ is Mears’ test with $Pe=2$, first order, 99 % conversion

$$\frac{L}{d_p}>\frac{20\,n}{Pe}\,\ln\frac{C_{A0}}{C_A}$$
$n=1$, $Pe=2$, $x=0.99$: $\ \dfrac{20}{2}\ln 100=46\approx50$
the rule of thumb
  • Meaning: the bed volume is within 5 % of plug flow.
  • The rule fails when $Pe$ is small (liquids, slow lab beds) or conversion is very high: then use the test itself.

Rule 1 · axial mixing · step 2 of 2 · try it

High conversion and a low Peclet number demand a long bed

Mears$\dfrac{L}{d_p}>\dfrac{20n}{Pe_m}\ln\dfrac{1}{1-x}$
required $L/d_p$–

At 99.9 % conversion with $Pe=2$ the bed needs about 70 particle diameters; at $Pe=0.1$ it needs 1400: why short lab beds mislead.

Rule 2 · radial · step 1 of 2

$d_t/d_p>25$: the wall stops disturbing the flow

  • Next to the wall pellets pack loosely: gas runs faster there.
  • Radial Peclet $Pe_{mr}=ud_p/D_r\approx8.5\,[1+19.4(d_p/d_t)^2]$: the bracket is the wall effect.
  • Above $d_t/d_p=25$ it is about 3 %: flat velocity, and radial mass gradients are negligible.

The wall effect falls with the square of $d_t/d_p$: from 78 % at 5 to 3 % at 25, which is where the rule comes from.

Rule 2 · radial · step 2 of 2

Radial heat decides 1D or 2D: a thin, fast tube stays nearly flat

  • Adiabatic bed: no wall heat, no radial profile, always 1D.
  • Cooled tube: keep $d_t\le25$ mm (1 in) and $G$ high; 75–150 mm tubes need 2D. General test: Mears (1971), on the selection slide.

Rule 4 · pores

Pores: Weisz–Prater uses only measured numbers

Weisz–Prater$C_{WP}=\dfrac{r'_{obs}\rho_c(d_p/2)^2}{D_eC_{As}}$
Kinetics, isothermalNegligible if
zero order$C_{WP}<6$
first order$C_{WP}<1$
second order$C_{WP}<0.5$
power law, order $n$$C_{WP}<1/|n|$
  • Measure $r'_{obs}$ in the lab; $\rho_c$, $d_p$ known.
  • $D_e$: gas in pores about $10^{-6}$ m²/s; liquids $10^{-9}$ or less.
  • $C_{WP}\gg1$: crush the pellet or raise the pore size.
  • Lab and plant use the same pellet: the measured rate already includes $\eta$, so the rule needs no number.

Rule 3 · film

Film: rate over film transfer below 0.15, for mass and for heat

mass: $\dfrac{r'_{obs}\rho_c\,(d_p/2)\,n}{k_cC_{Ab}}<0.15$    heat: $\left|\dfrac{\Delta H\,r'_{obs}\rho_c(d_p/2)\,E}{h\,T_b^2R}\right|<0.15$
each keeps the rate within 5 %
$k_c$ from $j_D=\dfrac{Sh}{Re\,Sc^{1/3}}=\dfrac{k_c}{u}Sc^{2/3}\approx\dfrac{0.357}{\varepsilon}Re^{-0.359}$ (gas)
$j_D$: Colburn factor, a dimensionless $k_c$
  • $k_c$ and $h$ rise with gas velocity: hence the rule $G>1.35$ kg/m²s.
  • $h$ follows from $j_H=j_D$ (heat–mass analogy).

Rules 3–4 · try it

Four numbers decide the mass and heat level of the model

Fixed: $\rho_c=2500$, $C=0.6825$ mol/m³, $T=893$ K, $E=144$ kJ/mol, $\Delta H=124.8$ kJ/mol, $\lambda_s=0.2$, $n=1$. Defaults: a styrene lab bed (Froment Ex. 11.7).

Halving $d_p$ cuts $C_{WP}$ four times but the film ratios only two times (at fixed $k_c$, $h$): pellet size is the first lever for internal limits, flow velocity for external.

Choosing the model · try it

Four questions, in order, give the model code

1 · Axial mixing

rule $L/d_p>50$  test $\frac{L}{d_p}>\frac{20n}{Pe}\ln\frac{C_0}{C}$

2 · Radial heat

rule adiabatic, or $d_t\le25$ mm & high $G$  test Mears radial

3 · Film

rule $G>1.35$ kg/m²s  test Mears, both < 0.15

4 · Pores

rule same pellet as the lab  test $C_{WP}<1/|n|$

A-Iplug flow A-II+ axial mixing A-III+ radial, 2D B-I+ film B-II+ film and pores B-III+ film, 2D

All four pass: A-I, the model of most plants. Each failure adds one effect; radial heat, not $d_t/d_p$, decides 1D against 2D.

Section 15-3 · summary

Pick the flow level and the pellet level; the rules usually give A-I

  • Flow: plug flow (I) → axial mixing (II) → radial, 2D (III). Pellet: one phase (A) or gas and catalyst apart (B).
  • Rules: $L/d_p>50$, $d_t/d_p>25$ with a thin cooled tube, $G>1.35$ kg/m²s, same pellet as the lab.
  • Outside ordinary gas beds, use the tests behind the rules.

Code chosen. Next: write its balances, one term at a time.

How do we write the model of a fixed bed?

Start from the slice balance of Lectures 5 and 7, then add one term per level of 15-3.

In − out + generation = accumulationPressure dropHeat to the wallAdding terms

Lecture 15-4

One slice, one balance, one more term at each step

  1. Model A-Imole and energy balance on a slice $dz$, each term named
  2. Pressure dropErgun, and one worked example
  3. Heat to the wall$U$, and why the wall coefficient depends on $d_p$
  4. Adding termsA-II, A-III, B-I: what each adds to A-I

Model A-I · step 1 of 3

Every balance in this lecture is one sentence, written on a slice $dz$

$$\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\text{in}}\;-\;\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\text{out}}\;+\;\textcolor{#15803D}{\text{generation}}\;=\;\textcolor{#6B7280}{\text{accumulation}}$$

Colours from here on: flow navy, reaction green, wall heat red, storage grey.

Model A-I · step 2 of 3 · mole balance

Mole balance: flow in minus flow out plus reaction

$\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{F_i\big|_z}-\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{F_i\big|_{z+dz}}+\textcolor{#15803D}{\nu_ir'\,\rho_BA_c\,dz}=\textcolor{#6B7280}{0}$
steady state; $\rho_BA_cdz$ = catalyst mass in the slice
$F_i=uA_cC_i$; divide by $A_c\,dz$: $\quad \textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}}=\textcolor{#15803D}{\rho_B\,\nu_ir'}$
same as $dF_i/dW=\nu_ir'$ of Lecture 5
unsteady: add $\textcolor{#6B7280}{\varepsilon\,\dfrac{\partial C_i}{\partial t}}$ on the left
gas held in the voids

$\rho_B=(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s$: catalyst per bed volume.

Model A-I · step 3 of 3 · energy balance

Energy: $\dot m c_pT$ in minus out, plus heat of reaction, minus heat to the wall

$\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\dot m c_pT\big|_z}-\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\dot m c_pT\big|_{z+dz}}+\textcolor{#15803D}{(-\Delta H)\,r'\rho_BA_c\,dz}-\textcolor{#C00000}{U\,\pi d_t\,dz\,(T-T_c)}=\textcolor{#6B7280}{0}$
$\dot m=GA_c$, kg/s
divide by $A_c\,dz$: $\quad \textcolor{#1E3A8A}{G\,c_p\dfrac{dT}{dz}}=\textcolor{#15803D}{(-\Delta H)\,\rho_B r'}-\textcolor{#C00000}{\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)}$
$\pi d_t/A_c=4/d_t$: wall area per bed volume

Model A-I · pressure

Ergun adds the laminar and the turbulent losses

$-\dfrac{dp}{dz}=f\,\dfrac{G^2}{\rho_g d_p},\qquad Re=\dfrac{G\,d_p}{\mu}$
friction form; $G$ constant by continuity
laminar: $f=\dfrac{(1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3}\dfrac{150}{Re}$  ·  turbulent: $f=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^3}\,1.75$
Hagen–Poiseuille with tortuosity fit; Burke–Plummer
$f=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^3}\Big[1.75+\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon)}{Re}\Big]$
Ergun (1952): sum of both

$d_p$: sphere of the same area per volume, $d_p=6(1-\varepsilon)/a_v$. Valid for $Re/(1-\varepsilon)<500$.

Pressure drop · try it

Smaller pellets and higher mass flux cost pressure fast

Ergun$-\dfrac{dp}{dz}=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^3}\Big[1.75+\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon)}{Re}\Big]\dfrac{G^2}{\rho_gd_p}$
$Re$–
$\Delta P/L$ (Pa/m)–
turbulent share–

Air at 372 °C. Design band 2470–4490 Pa/m and $\Delta P<10\%$ of the inlet pressure; at high $Re$ the drop grows with $G^2/d_p$.

Example 15.1 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 15.1Pressure drop in a packed tube

A tube with a length 2.5 m and an internal diameter 0.025 m is packed with alumina cylinders with a diameter and height 0.003 m. The void fraction of the bed is $\varepsilon=0.38$. Air flows through the tube at 372°C with a superficial mass flow velocity of 1.3 kg/m² s. Calculate the pressure drop in the bed. Viscosity of air at 372°C = 0.031 cps = 3.1 × 10−5 kg/m s; specific mass of air at 372°C = 0.9487 kg/m³.

Example 15.1 · solution

EXAMPLE 15.1$\Delta P=0.32$ bar over 2.5 m, about 30 % of an atmosphere

Ergun$f=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^3}\Big[1.75+\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon)}{Re}\Big],\quad \Delta P=f\,\dfrac{\rho_gu_s^2L}{d_p}$
$u_s=\dfrac{1.3}{0.9487}=1.37$ m/s,  $d_p=0.0037$ m,  $Re=\dfrac{0.0037\times1.3}{3.1\times10^{-5}}=155$
equal-area sphere, as in the book
$f=\dfrac{0.62}{0.38^3}\Big[1.75+\dfrac{150\times0.62}{155}\Big]=26.5$
Ergun friction factor
$\Delta P=26.5\times\dfrac{0.9487\times1.37^2\times2.5}{0.0037}=3.19\times10^4$ Pa $=0.319$ bar
recomputed: matches

The book uses $d_p=\sqrt{1.5}\,d=0.0037$ m. Its own rule $d_p=6(1-\varepsilon)/a_v$ gives $d_p=d=0.003$ m and $\Delta P=0.42$ bar.

The red term needs $U$: three resistances in series between the bed and the coolant.

Heat to the wall · step 1 of 3

$U$ adds three resistances: bed side, wall, coolant side

$$\frac1U=\frac1{\alpha_i}+\frac{d}{\lambda}\frac{A_b}{A_m}+\frac1{\alpha_u}\frac{A_b}{A_u}$$
  • Coolant side (boiling water, molten salt) and the steel wall are small resistances.
  • The bed side $\alpha_i$ usually controls: about 100–300 W/m²K, from Leva’s correlation:
cooling $\dfrac{\alpha_id_t}{\lambda_g}=3.50\,Re^{0.7}e^{-4.6d_p/d_t}$;   heating $0.813\,Re^{0.9}e^{-6d_p/d_t}$
$Re=d_pG/\mu$
$\alpha_i$, $\alpha_u$
film coefficient, bed side; coolant side
W/m²K
$d$, $\lambda$
wall thickness; wall conductivity
m, W/m K

Heat to the wall · step 2 of 3 · Auxiliary relations · $\alpha$ against $h_p$

Two films, two coefficients: around every pellet, and along the wall

$h_p$ (and $k_p$)$\alpha_w$, $\alpha_i$
interfacegas → pellet surfacebed → tube wall
drives$T-T_s$ in the heterogeneous model (B)$T-T_{wall}$; part of $U$ in the 1D model, boundary condition of the 2D
area it acts on$\rho_Ba_g$, about 1000 m²/m³ of bed$4/d_t$, about 160 m²/m³ for 2.5 cm
from$j_H=f(Re_p)$, Colburn analogy with $k_p$Leva; De Wasch–Froment: $\alpha_w=\alpha_w^0+c\,Re$
typical100–500 W/m²K100–200 W/m²K; $\alpha_i$ lumps the core resistance too

Same physics, different surfaces: $h_p$ belongs to the heterogeneous model, $\alpha$ to a cooled tube.

Heat to the wall · step 3 of 3 · try it

$\alpha_i$ rises with $G$, and peaks at a pellet size near $d_t/6.5$

$Re$–
$\alpha_i$ cooling–
$\alpha_i$ heating–
  • Why $d_p$: bigger pellets stir the gas at the wall ($Re^{0.7}$) but pack loosely there ($e^{-4.6d_p/d_t}$): a maximum.
  • Heating vs cooling: Leva fitted separate experiments; likely because near-wall gas viscosity shifts the opposite way. Use the one matching the duty.

At $G=1.3$, $d_t=2.54$ cm cooling gives $\alpha_i\approx110$ W/m²K, close to $U=96$ used for the o-xylene tube.

A-I is complete. Each level of 15-3 now adds one term to it.

Adding terms · A-II · step 1 of 3

A-II: axial mixing adds a second derivative, in blue

$0=-\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}}+\textcolor{#2563EB}{\varepsilon D_a\dfrac{d^2C_i}{dz^2}}+\textcolor{#15803D}{\rho_B\nu_ir'}$
mass
$0=-\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{Gc_p\dfrac{dT}{dz}}+\textcolor{#2563EB}{\lambda_a\dfrac{d^2T}{dz^2}}+\textcolor{#15803D}{(-\Delta H)\rho_Br'}-\textcolor{#C00000}{\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)}$
energy

A second derivative needs two boundary conditions: Danckwerts, as in Lecture 12.

2D needs the bed’s radial conductivity $\lambda_{er}$: what is the conductivity of a bed that is half gas?

Adding terms · A-III · step 2 of 3

Four heat paths across a bed, lumped into one conductivity

$$\lambda_{er}=\underbrace{\lambda^0_{er}}_{\text{static, paths 1–3}}+\underbrace{\lambda^t_{er}}_{\text{dynamic, path 4}}$$
  • Static: no flow; set by $\varepsilon$, $\lambda_s/\lambda_g$, contacts, radiation above 400 °C.
  • Dynamic: the flow carries heat sideways as it carries mass; grows with $Re$.
  • $\lambda$ or $k$? Same quantity. Fogler writes $k_e$; Froment uses $\lambda$ since $k$ is the rate constant.

Adding terms · A-III · step 2 of 3

A-III: radial mixing in teal; the wall heat moves into a boundary condition

$0=-\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{Gc_p\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial z}}+\textcolor{#0F766E}{\lambda_{er}\Big(\dfrac{\partial^2T}{\partial r^2}+\dfrac1r\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial r}\Big)}+\textcolor{#15803D}{(-\Delta H)\rho_Br'}$
energy; mass alike with $\varepsilon D_r$
$r=0$: $\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial r}=0$;   $r=R$: $\textcolor{#C00000}{-\lambda_{er}\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial r}=\alpha_w(T-T_w)}$
symmetry; heat leaves at the wall

No $4U/d_t$ term: the wall loss is now the condition at $r=R$.

Adding terms · B-I · step 3 of 3

B-I: gas and catalyst each get a balance, joined by the film (orange)

gas: $\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}}=-\textcolor{#C2410C}{\rho_Bk_pa_g(C_i-C_{s,i})}$
mass
gas: $\textcolor{#1E3A8A}{Gc_p\dfrac{dT}{dz}}=\textcolor{#C2410C}{\rho_Bh_pa_g(T_s-T)}-\textcolor{#C00000}{\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)}$
energy
catalyst: $\textcolor{#C2410C}{k_pa_g(C_i-C_{s,i})}=-\textcolor{#15803D}{\nu_ir'(C_s,T_s)}$
supply = use
catalyst: $\textcolor{#C2410C}{h_pa_g(T_s-T)}=\textcolor{#15803D}{(-\Delta H)r'}$
heat made = heat out

Balance terms · which model uses which

Six terms build every model in the family

TermMaterialEnergyNeeded by
Convection$-\partial(uC_i)/\partial z$$-G\,c_{pg}\,\partial T/\partial z$A-I every model
Reaction$(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,\nu_ir'$$(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,\nu_ir'(-\Delta H_{R_i})$A-I every model
Dispersion, axial$\varepsilon D_{a,i}\,\partial^2C_i/\partial z^2$$\lambda_a\,\partial^2T/\partial z^2$A-II
Dispersion, radial$\varepsilon D_{r,i}\big(\partial^2C_i/\partial r^2+\tfrac1r\partial C_i/\partial r\big)$$\lambda_r\big(\partial^2T/\partial r^2+\tfrac1r\partial T/\partial r\big)$A-III B-III
Gas–solid transfer$\rho_Bk_{p,i}a_g(C_i-C_{s,i})$$\rho_Bh_pa_g(T_s-T)$B only fluid ↔ solid
Storage$(\varepsilon+(1-\varepsilon)\varepsilon_p)\,\partial C_i/\partial t$$(\varepsilon\rho_gc_{pg}+(1-\varepsilon)\rho_sc_{ps})\,\partial T/\partial t$transient any model

A pseudo-homogeneous: one phase, $T=T_s$. B heterogeneous adds the transfer row and a second (solid) balance. Wall heat: $-4U(T-T_c)/d_t$ in 1D, boundary condition in 2D.

Adding terms · conditions

Steady state needs only inlet conditions; transients need a starting profile

Basic model A-I$\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}=(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\nu_ir',\quad Gc_{pg}\dfrac{dT}{dz}=(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\nu_ir'(-\Delta H_{R_i})-\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)$
Plug flow: $z=0$: $C_i=C_{i0}$, $T=T_0$, $p=p_0$
initial-value problem
Dispersion: Danckwerts at $z=0$ and $z=L$
two-point boundary value problem
Heterogeneous: the same conditions on the gas phase
solid has no flow term
  • Start-up: $C_i=0$, $T=$ ambient throughout.
  • Disturbance or shut-down: start from the steady-state profiles.

Section 15-4 · summary

A-I from one slice; every other model adds a coloured term

  • A-I: $d(uC_i)/dz=\rho_B\nu_ir'$; $Gc_p\,dT/dz=(-\Delta H)\rho_Br'-4U(T-T_c)/d_t$; Ergun for $p$.
  • $U$ is set by the bed side $\alpha_i$: up with $G$, best near $d_t/d_p\approx7$.
  • A-II adds $\varepsilon D_a$, $\lambda_a$; A-III adds $\varepsilon D_r$, $\lambda_{er}$ and a wall condition; B adds a catalyst balance.

Kinetics are measured once, then reworked from pilot data before the final sizing: the model is refined as the evidence grows.

Design sequence · model choice

The model choice depends on the job, not on the reactor alone

StageSizingMultiplicity, sensitivityStability
1. PreliminaryA-I steady 1D plug flow, pseudo-homogeneous––
2. Pilot reactorA-II steady 1D dispersion; A-III 2D if heat effects are largeas for sizingA-Itransient 1D plug flow
3. Final designA-III steady 2D dispersion, pseudo-homogeneousas for sizingA-IItransient 1D dispersion
  • APseudo-homogeneous: widely used; heat and mass transfer much faster than reaction.
  • BHeterogeneous: rarely; when the reaction is very fast. B-III2D heterogeneous: rarely; too many parameters — counted next.

Design sequence · parameters · step 1 of 2

Five kinds of parameter, from five different places

KindExamplesWhere it comes fromConfidence
Kinetic, thermodynamic$k_0$, $E$, rate form, $\Delta H$, $K_{eq}$lab kinetics (Lecture 8); thermochemistrygood, if measured on the final catalyst
Design choices$d_t$, $L$, $d_p$, $\varepsilon$, $\rho_B$chosen by the designer, then measuredexact
Operating$G$, $C_0$, $T_0$, $p_0$, $T_c$process specificationexact
Fluid properties$\rho_g$, $c_{pg}$, $\mu$, $\lambda_g$, $D_m$handbook, property package±5 %
Effective transport$U$, $\alpha_w$, $D_a$, $\lambda_a$, $D_r$, $\lambda_r$, $k_p$, $h_p$, $D_e$, $\lambda_e$$Re$-correlations (15-3, 15-4), pellet tortuosity±20–50 %

Only the last kind changes with the model. "Too many parameters" means too many effective transport values, each uncertain by tens of percent.

A-I needs one transport value, $U$; B-III needs seven, each ±20–50 % — the final-design choice is A-III, where only three are needed and all three come from one $Re$.

Example 15.2 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 15.2Preliminary design: thermal cracking of propane

Thermal cracking of propane in the presence of steam in an open tubular reactor in a cracking furnace providing a uniform, constant heat flux to the tube wall.

Information available: tube diameter (10.8 cm) and length (95 m; the source text prints 9.5 m); heat flux per m of tube length; kinetic scheme: 7 reactions with rate constants and activation energies; heat of reaction (+103,800 kJ/kmol).

Design question: can a C3 conversion ($X$) of 60 % be achieved at a specified feed rate with 0.4 kg steam/kg C3 and an inlet temperature of 680 °C and an inlet pressure of 2.93 bars?

Example 15.2 · solution, model · step 1 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.2The Lecture 5 tubular balance, written per metre of an open tube

Lecture 5 · tubular reactor design equation$\dfrac{dF_j}{dV}=\sum_k\nu_{jk}\,r_k,\qquad dV=A_c\,dz$
$\dfrac{1}{A_c}\dfrac{dF_j}{dz}=\sum_k\nu_{jk}\,r_k$
no catalyst: $r_k$ is per m³ of gas, kmol/m³s
$\dfrac{d(uC_j)}{dz}=\sum_{k=1}^{7}\nu_{jk}\,r_k$
$F_j=A_c\,u\,C_j$; one line for each species, seven reactions
$0=-\dfrac{d(uC_j)}{dz}+\sum_k\nu_{jk}\,r_k$
same form as A-I with $(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s r'\to r$: an empty tube is the limit $\varepsilon=1$

$u$ changes along the tube: moles grow with cracking, $p_t$ falls, $T$ rises.

Example 15.2 · solution, model · step 2 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.2The Lecture 7 energy balance, with the furnace flux as $\dot Q$

Lecture 7 · energy balance$\Big(\sum_iN_iC_{p,i}\Big)\dfrac{dT}{dt}=\dot Q+\dot W_s-\sum_jr_jV\Delta H_{Rxj}-\sum_iF_{i0}C_{p,i}(T-T_F)$
$0=\dot Q-\sum_kr_kA_c\Delta z\,\Delta H_{Rk}-\sum_iF_iC_{p,i}\big[T(z+\Delta z)-T(z)\big]$
slice $A_c\Delta z$, steady, $\dot W_s=0$; the slice’s feed arrives at $T(z)$
$\dot Q=q\,\pi d_t\,\Delta z,\qquad \sum_iF_iC_{p,i}=A_c\,G\,c_{pg}$
$q$: heat flux on the wall, fixed by the furnace, not by $T$
$0=-Gc_{pg}\dfrac{dT}{dz}+\sum_kr_k(-\Delta H_{Rk})+\dfrac{4q}{d_t}$
divide by $A_c\Delta z$, $\Delta z\to0$; $\pi d_t/A_c=4/d_t$

Cracking is endothermic: $\sum r_k(-\Delta H_{Rk})<0$, and only the furnace term keeps $T$ rising.

Example 15.2 · solution, model · step 3 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.21D plug flow, steady, seven reactions, plus a pressure equation

$0=-\dfrac{d(uC_j)}{dz}+\sum_k\nu_{jk}\,r_k$
material, each species (step 1)
$0=-Gc_{pg}\dfrac{dT}{dz}+\sum_kr_k(-\Delta H_{Rk})+\dfrac{4q}{d_t}$
energy; furnace flux $q$ replaces $U(T_c-T)$ (step 2)
$-\dfrac{dp_t}{dz}=\dfrac{2f\,G^2}{\rho_g\,d_t}$,   $z=0$: $C_j=C_{j0}$, $T=T_0$, $p_t=p_{t0}$
Fanning friction in an empty tube; inlet conditions

In the packed-bed form of 15-4 this is A-I with $(1-\varepsilon)\rho_sr'$ read as the gas-phase rate $r$.

Example 15.2 · solution, choosing the model

EXAMPLE 15.2Why A-I is enough here: every question of 15-3 answers “no”

Question of 15-3HereSo
Pellet level: film? pores?no catalyst: cracking happens in the gas itselfA exactly, one phase
Axial mixing?empty tube, turbulent, $L/d_t\approx880\gg10$; $D/uL\approx3\times10^{-4}$plug flow
Radial profile?turbulent core mixes; endothermic, so no hot spot to resolve1D
AnswerA-I steady 1D plug flow, pseudo-homogeneous: the preliminary-sizing model of the design table

The source’s own reason: $L/d_T=90$ (it prints 9.5 m), so plug flow; with 95 m the case is stronger. The plant data on the next slides confirm it.

Example 15.2 · solution, results · try it

EXAMPLE 15.2The furnace flux decides the answer: about 31 kW/m² gives 60 %

$x$ at 95 m–
$T_{out}$ (°C)–
$p_{out}$ (bar)–

Model at $q=31.24$: $x=0.600$, 766 °C, 2.43 bar. Plant: 60 %, about 835 °C, 1.4 bar.

Yes, 60 % is reachable; the flux, not the tube, sets the conversion. One global reaction misses the plant’s hotter outlet and its larger pressure drop from the bends.

Example 15.2 · solution, result

EXAMPLE 15.2Yes: 60 % at the outlet; the source’s 7-reaction A-I model matches the plant

  • Conversion reaches 60 % at the outlet.
  • Temperature: a fast rise to about 770 °C, then a slow climb to about 835 °C.
  • Pressure falls from 2.93 to about 1.4 bar.
  • Plug flow works because $L/d_t$ is large.

Source figure, with plant data as markers; the source states $L=9.5$ m, $L/d_t=90$, but its axis runs to 95 m.

Example 15.3 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 15.3Pilot design: o-xylene to phthalic anhydride

Synthesis of phthalic anhydride (PA) with the partial oxidation of o-xylene (o-X) in air over a supported V2O5 catalyst.

$r'=k'_{app}P^0_{O_2}P_{ox}$,   $P^0_{O_2}=0.211$ bar,   $\ln k'_{app}=19.837-\dfrac{13636}{T}$

Tube diameter (2.54 cm) and length (3 m); catalyst particle size $d_p=3$ mm; coolant is a molten salt at 352 °C.

Design question: what is the o-X conversion for a 1 m deep catalyst bed where the first 2 m of tube length brings the gas temperature to 352 °C? Initial partial pressure of o-X = 0.01 bar and oxygen = 0.211 bar. What are the o-xylene concentration profile and the temperature profile in the bed?

$\rho_B$1300 kg/m³
$G$4684 kg/m²h (1.30 kg/m²s)
$(-\Delta H)$1 285 409 kJ/kmol
$c_p$0.992 kJ/kg K
$U$0.096 kJ/m²s K

Example 15.3 · solution, model · step 1 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.3The Lecture 5 packed bed balance becomes the gas mass balance

Lecture 5 · packed bed design equation$\dfrac{dF_j}{dW}=\sum_i\nu_{ij}r'_i,\qquad dW=(1-\Phi)A_c\rho_c\,dz$
$\dfrac{dF_i}{dW}=\nu_i\,r'$
one reaction, o-xylene → PA; here $\Phi\to\varepsilon$, $\rho_c\to\rho_s$
$\dfrac{1}{A_c}\dfrac{dF_i}{dz}=(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,\nu_i\,r'$
$dW/dz=(1-\varepsilon)A_c\rho_s$: catalyst per metre
$\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}=(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,\nu_i\,r'$
plug flow: $F_i=A_c\,u\,C_i$ ⇒ model A-I
$0=-\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}+\boxed{\varepsilon D_a\dfrac{d^2C_i}{dz^2}}+(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,\nu_i\,r'$
add the dispersive flux: $F_i=A_c\big(uC_i-\varepsilon D_a\,dC_i/dz\big)$ ⇒ A-II

Example 15.3 · solution, model · step 2 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.3The Lecture 7 energy balance, written for one slice of the bed

Lecture 7 · energy balance$\Big(\sum_iN_iC_{p,i}\Big)\dfrac{dT}{dt}=\dot Q+\dot W_s-\sum_jr_jV\Delta H_{Rxj}-\sum_iF_{i0}C_{p,i}(T-T_F)$
$0=\dot Q-r'\rho_BA_c\Delta z\,\Delta H_{Rx}-\sum_iF_iC_{p,i}\big[T(z+\Delta z)-T(z)\big]$
slice $A_c\Delta z$, steady, $\dot W_s=0$; the slice’s feed is the gas arriving at $T(z)$
$\dot Q=U\,\pi d_t\Delta z\,(T_c-T),\qquad \sum_iF_iC_{p,i}=A_c\,G\,c_{pg}$
heat through the tube wall; molar to mass flux
$G\,c_{pg}\dfrac{dT}{dz}=(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,r'(-\Delta H_{Rx})-\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)$
divide by $A_c\Delta z$, $\Delta z\to0$; $\pi d_t/A_c=4/d_t$ ⇒ A-I
$0=-Gc_{pg}\dfrac{dT}{dz}+\boxed{\lambda_a\dfrac{d^2T}{dz^2}}+(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,r'(-\Delta H_{Rx})-\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)$
add axial conduction, flux $-\lambda_a\,dT/dz$ ⇒ A-II

Example 15.3 · solution, model · step 3 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.31D dispersion, pseudo-homogeneous, with Danckwerts conditions

Steps 1 and 2: model A-II$0=-\dfrac{d(uC_i)}{dz}+\varepsilon D_a\dfrac{d^2C_i}{dz^2}+(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\nu_ir'$$0=-Gc_{pg}\dfrac{dT}{dz}+\lambda_a\dfrac{d^2T}{dz^2}+(1-\varepsilon)\rho_s\,r'(-\Delta H_{Rx})-\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)$
$z=0$: $u(C_{i0}-C_i)=-\varepsilon D_a\dfrac{dC_i}{dz}$, $\ \rho_guc_p(T_0-T)=-\lambda_a\dfrac{dT}{dz}$;   $z=L$: zero gradients
Danckwerts

Parameters: $D_a$ from the $Pe$–$Re$ chart, $U$ from Leva, $\Delta P$ from Ergun.

Example 15.3 · solution, results · pick a profile

EXAMPLE 15.3Dispersion changes nothing; the pressure drop does

A-IA-IIA-I + Ergun
$p_{oX}$ out (atm)0.007150.007150.00581
conversion $x$0.2850.2850.214
$T_{max}$ (K)636.8636.8635.1
at $z$ (m)0.390.390.29
$\Delta P$ (bar)0.23–0.26

$D/uL=0.0015$, far below 0.01. Ergun with $\varepsilon=0.40$ (assumed).

A-I and A-II lie on top of each other. A 0.26 bar drop at 1 atm cuts both partial pressures: conversion falls from 28.5 % to 21 %.

Example 15.3 · solution, result

EXAMPLE 15.3About 21–29 % conversion: dispersion changes nothing, pressure drop does

  • Source ($p_0=0.011$, $p_{O_2}=0.208$ atm): outlet 0.0077 atm, about 30 %: the isobaric A-I answer. Low conversion per pass is typical of partial oxidation.
  • Model, isobaric: 0.00715 atm, 28.5 %, for both A-I and A-II. $L/d_p=333$, $D/uL=0.0015$: 1D plug flow is enough.
  • Ergun at 625 K, 1 atm: about 0.23 bar over 1 m at inlet density, 0.26 bar coupled. Coupled to the rate, conversion falls to 21 %.
  • The 2D model that follows keeps it isobaric too, so the two can be compared term for term.

The source calls the pressure drop “very small”; at 1 atm it is not. Check $\varepsilon$ and $P_t$ before relying on either number.

Example 15.3 · try it

Faster gas: less conversion per tube, a lower hot spot

outlet $p_{oX}$ (bar)–
$x$–

1D plug flow, $p_0=0.01$ bar, $T_0=T_c=625$ K; $\Delta P$ with $\varepsilon=0.40$ assumed.

Mass flux trades conversion per tube against heat removal: halving $G$ doubles the residence time and raises the hot spot.

Final design: is the temperature really uniform across a cooled tube?

Going 2D · step 1 of 2

Heat leaves through the wall, so the axis runs hotter than the mean

  • Effective transport: radial flux $=-\lambda_{er}\,\partial T/\partial r$ and $-\varepsilon D_{er}\,\partial C/\partial r$, on top of plug flow.
  • $Pe_{mr}=ud_p/D_{er}\approx8$–$10$: radial mass mixing is good.
  • $\lambda_{er}$ and the wall coefficient $\alpha_w$ set the radial temperature drop.
  • o-xylene, $d_t=2.54$ cm: the axis is well above the mean at the hot spot; results are very sensitive to $\lambda_{er}$, $\alpha_w$, much less to $Pe_{mr}$.

Going 2D · step 2 of 2 · try it

Wide tube, hot core: the axis rise grows with the radius squared

core: $\ T_{axis}-T_{wall}=\dfrac{Q\,R^2}{4\lambda_{er}}$
conduction
film: $\ T_{wall}-T_c=\dfrac{Q\,R}{2\alpha_w}$
wall film
core rise (K)–
film rise (K)–

Fixed: $Q=160$ kW/m³ (o-xylene hot spot), $\alpha_w=200$ W/m²K. Grey: the 2.54 cm tube.

Doubling $d_t$ quadruples the core rise but only doubles the film rise; a higher $\lambda_{er}$ flattens the core. Small core rise: lump it into one $\alpha_i$ and stay 1D.

Example 15.3 continued · final design, 2D · step 1 of 3

EXAMPLE 15.3Add radial conduction and dispersion to the A-I balances: model A-III

Example 15.3, A-I$u_0\dfrac{dp}{dz}=-\dfrac{\rho_BM_mP_t}{\rho_g}r',\qquad Gc_p\dfrac{dT}{dz}=\rho_B(-\Delta H)r'-\dfrac{4U}{d_t}(T-T_c)$
$u_0\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial z}=\varepsilon D_{er}\Big(\dfrac{\partial^2p}{\partial r^2}+\dfrac1r\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial r}\Big)-\dfrac{\rho_BM_mP_t}{\rho_g}r'$
mass on a ring $2\pi r\,\Delta r\,\Delta z$; radial flux $-\varepsilon D_{er}\,\partial p/\partial r$
$Gc_p\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial z}=\lambda_{er}\Big(\dfrac{\partial^2T}{\partial r^2}+\dfrac1r\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial r}\Big)+\rho_B(-\Delta H)r'$
same ring; the wall term $4U/d_t$ leaves the equation…
$r=0:\ \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial r}=\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial r}=0;\qquad r=R_t:\ \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial r}=0,\ \ -\lambda_{er}\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial r}=\alpha_w(T-T_c)$
…and comes back as the wall boundary condition

Book data: $\lambda_{er}=0.78$ W/m K, $\alpha_w=156$ W/m²K, $Pe_{mr}=10$. Check: $1/U=1/\alpha_w+R_t/4\lambda_{er}$ gives $U=95.4$, the 96 of the 1D model.

EXAMPLE 15.3When does the 2D map collapse to the 1D model?

Large $\lambda_{er}$, a thin tube or a lean feed flatten the radial profile and the 2D map becomes the 1D A-I model with $1/U=1/\alpha_w+R_t/4\lambda_{er}$; a rich feed in a wide tube does the opposite.

Section 15-5 · summary

Use the simplest model that answers the question of the stage

  • Preliminary: 1D plug flow. Pilot: 1D dispersion, 2D if heat effects are large. Final: 2D.
  • Propane cracking ($L/d_t\approx880$) and o-xylene ($L/d_p=333$): long beds, so plug flow already matches.
  • Radial $T$ profiles appear whenever heat crosses the wall; $\lambda_{er}$ and $\alpha_w$ govern them.
  • Equivalent 1D: $1/\alpha_i=1/\alpha_w+R_t/4\lambda_{er}$.

Problem 15.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 15.1Axial dispersion coefficient in a lab-scale bed

(Fixed reactor, 5 pts) Determine the axial dispersion coefficient in the gas phase lab-scale fixed bed reactor. The powder of catalyst with a diameter 250 µm. The reactor height is 3 cm with a diameter 2 cm. The bed density is 1400 kg/m³ with void fraction at 0.45. The reactor inlet gas density and viscosity are 0.37 kg/m³ and 0.035 cP, respectively. The inlet gas superficial velocity is 0.05 m/s. The Schmidt number of gas at 0.35 is assumed.

$d_p$250 µm
$L$, $d_t$3 cm, 2 cm
$\varepsilon$0.45
$\rho_g$, $\mu$0.37 kg/m³, 0.035 cP
$u$0.05 m/s
$Sc$0.35

Read $D\varepsilon/ud_p$ from the axial dispersion chart, gas curve, against $Re$; the chart is on the next slide.

Problem 15.1 · solution

PROBLEM 15.1$D=6.9\times10^{-5}$ m²/s; $D\varepsilon/uL=0.021$, so dispersion is not negligible

Definitions$Re=\dfrac{d_pu\rho_g}{\mu},\ \ y=\dfrac{D\varepsilon}{ud_p},\ \ \dfrac{D}{uL}$
$Re=\dfrac{d_pu\rho_g}{\mu}=\dfrac{250\times10^{-6}\times0.05\times0.37}{3.5\times10^{-5}}=0.132$
particle Reynolds number
Chart, gas $Sc=0.35$: $\dfrac{D\varepsilon}{ud_p}\approx2.5$ (fit $0.452\,Re^{-0.842}$)
low $Re$: diffusion dominates
$D=\dfrac{2.5\times0.05\times250\times10^{-6}}{0.45}=6.94\times10^{-5}$ m²/s
solve for $D$
$\dfrac{D}{u_iL}=\dfrac{D\varepsilon}{uL}=\dfrac{6.94\times10^{-5}\times0.45}{0.05\times0.03}=0.021>0.01$
$u_i=u/\varepsilon$; not plug flow

$L/d_p=120>50$, yet $Pe\approx0.4$ at $Re=0.13$: the rule of thumb fails; the test says dispersion matters.

Problem 15.1 · try it

$Re$–
$D$ (m²/s)–
$D/u_iL$–

$\rho_g=0.37$ kg/m³, $\mu=0.035$ cP, $\varepsilon=0.45$, $Sc=0.35$.

Chart, gas, fitted$\dfrac{D\varepsilon}{ud_p}\approx\max\big(0.5,\ 0.452\,Re^{-0.842}\big)$

Lab beds of fine powder at low velocity sit far above $D/u_iL=0.01$: their data need the dispersion model, or a longer bed.

Problem 15.2 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 15.2Which model for a commercial fixed bed?

The commercial scale fixed bed reactor was designed at 1 m diameter and 8 m length with 0.40 bed void fraction. Catalyst density and equivalent particle size were 1200 kg/m³ and 1.5 mm. From the pilot scale test, the apparent rate with first order kinetic of limiting reactant was obtained with the reaction rate constant $4.54\times10^{-5}$ m³/(kgcat s). The feed concentration was specified at 0.1 mol/L. From the flow rate in the reactor, the mass transfer coefficient $1.05\times10^{-4}$ m/s was calculated from the dimensionless correlation (Sh, Sc, Re). The heat of reaction is −150 kJ/mol. What is your suggested model for modelling this reactor? (Hint: Mears criteria $\dfrac{r'_{obs}\rho_b(d_p/2)n}{k_cC_{Ab}}<0.15$)

a. 1D pseudo-homogeneous model, axial dispersion   b. 1D heterogeneous model with axial dispersion   c. 1D heterogeneous model with plug flow   d. 2D pseudo-homogeneous model, plug flow   e. 2D pseudo-homogeneous model, axial dispersion

Problem 15.2 · solution

PROBLEM 15.2The film matters; axial dispersion does not

Mears, external mass$\dfrac{r'_{obs}\rho_b(d_p/2)\,n}{k_cC_{Ab}}<0.15$
$r'_{obs}=kC=4.54\times10^{-5}\times100=4.54\times10^{-3}$ mol/kg s,   $\rho_b=(1-0.40)\times1200=720$ kg/m³
$C=0.1$ mol/L $=100$ mol/m³
$\dfrac{4.54\times10^{-3}\times720\times0.00075\times1}{1.05\times10^{-4}\times100}=0.233>0.15$
external mass transfer matters: heterogeneous
$L/d_p=8/0.0015=5333\gg50$,   $d_t/d_p=667>25$
plug flow, flat velocity: 1D

Adiabatic 1 m vessel: no radial profile, so 1D. Density 1200 read as pellet density. Answer (c); the source key says (b).

Problem 15.2 · try it

Change the pellet, the film and the bed: watch the model class change

$k=4.54\times10^{-5}$ m³/kg s, $C=100$ mol/m³, $\rho_b=720$ kg/m³, $d_t=1$ m, $Pe=2$.

The film criterion, not the bed length, decides heterogeneous against pseudo-homogeneous here; dispersion appears only for very short beds.

Problem 15.3 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 15.3Dispersion coefficient in an esterification bed

Ethyl acetate is extensively used as a solvent. It is formed by the vapor-phase esterification of acetic acid and ethanol. The reaction was studied using a microporous resin as a catalyst in a packed-bed reactor. It is first-order in ethanol and pseudo-zero-order in acetic acid. For an equal molar feed rate of acetic acid and ethanol the specific reaction rate is 1.2 L/(g cat min). The total molar feed rate is 10 mol/min, the initial pressure is 10 atm, the temperature is 118 °C. Inlet superficial velocity at 1 m/s. Viscosity of feed 0.015 cP. Feed density 0.5 kg/m³. The size of microporous resin $d_p=2$ mm with void fraction = 0.50, particle density = 1600 kg/m³. What is the dispersion coefficient?

a. 0.001 m²/s   b. 0.02 m²/s   c. 0.002 m²/s   d. 0.02 m²/s   e. 0.1 m²/s

Problem 15.3 · solution

PROBLEM 15.3High-$Re$ gas: $D\varepsilon/ud_p\approx0.5$, so $D=0.002$ m²/s (c)

From Problem 15.1$Re=\dfrac{\rho ud_p}{\mu},\qquad \dfrac{D\varepsilon}{ud_p}=f(Re,Sc)\ \text{from the chart}$
$Re=\dfrac{\rho ud_p}{\mu}=\dfrac{0.5\times1\times0.002}{1.5\times10^{-5}}=66.7$
only the flow data are needed
Gas, $Re>2$: $\dfrac{D\varepsilon}{ud_p}\approx0.5$, i.e. $Pe\approx2$ on the interstitial velocity
the gas curves merge at high $Re$
$D=\dfrac{0.5\times1\times0.002}{0.50}=0.002$ m²/s
answer (c)

The kinetics are a distractor. Choices (b) and (d) are both 0.02 m²/s in the source; one was meant to differ.

Lecture 15

Key Takeaways

1

Pick the configuration from $\Delta T_{ad}$: one adiabatic bed, staged beds with intercooling or quench, or a cooled multitubular.

2

Name the model by two levels: flow (I plug flow, II axial, III radial) and pellet (A one phase, B gas and catalyst apart). Start from A-I.

3

Rules keep A-I: $L/d_p>50$, $d_t/d_p>25$ with a thin cooled tube, $G>1.35$ kg/m²s, the lab pellet. Outside ordinary gas beds, use the tests behind them.

4

Only the effective transport parameters change with the model, and each is uncertain by tens of percent: the simplest model that passes the criteria is the best one.

5

Design in stages: A-I to size, A-II for the pilot, A-III for the final tube — the 2D axis, not the 1D mean, sets the catalyst peak temperature.
